slides.title: Hurbuth Home Care wants to know who is likely to fall
slides.text: The case for four days Hurbuth Home Care wants to know who is likely to fall A fictional private provider of home nursing and physiotherapy for older people, in an unnamed city with five sectors A nurse assesses each client at home; the physiotherapy team can run a home programme for some of them The question: from the assessment, will this client fall in the next six months? Every record is synthetic; clients are codes, staff are roles Who decides what The clinical director owns the screen and approves its threshold. The physiotherapy team lead owns capacity. The quality and data protection officer reviews the model card. You are the data analyst who builds and tests it.

slides.title: Open a notebook, run the setup check
slides.text: Lab environment Open a notebook, run the setup check In a free hosted notebook service : open a lab from the course page; its first cell copies the course and installs the libraries it needs. On a laptop : clone the course, then run the commands on the right. Run 00_setup_check.ipynb. It prints the library versions and the number of assessments. No model is downloaded and no key is needed: every lab runs on a laptop processor in seconds. git clone https://github.com/SDAIAAcademy/fnd-aic-101 cd fnd-aic-101/labs uv sync uv run jupyter lab

slides.title: Your hands first, an assistant after
slides.text: How you may use AI assistants here Your hands first, an assistant after AI-off Every hand fit, the first attempt at each lab, and the supervised check at the end of the course. AI-tutor After your first attempt: an assistant may explain an error message or a library call. It does not write the exercise. AI-full The capstone code. You explain every line of it in the defence, and the trainer may ask you to re-run any result. Data. The course data is synthetic and published, so it may go into an assistant. At work, data classified Restricted or higher does not go into generative AI tools.

slides.title: Features, labels and prediction rules
slides.text: Session 1 Features, labels and prediction rules Name the identifier, the features and the label of a table of assessments Write a prediction rule as a function of the features Count a rule's two kinds of error on rows it was not written from 01

slides.title: Supervised learning starts from a table of solved examples
slides.text: Learning from examples Supervised learning starts from a table of solved examples A parallel case: the wound-care nurses of the same company want to know which dressing visits will run over 40 minutes. Wound area (cm²) Dressing layers Diabetic Ran over 40 min 28.5 1 0 0 7.6 4 0 0 7.4 1 1 0 22.1 4 0 1 25.1 3 0 1 30.6 4 1 1 Six synthetic wound-care visits (labs/_tools/teaching_examples.py).

slides.title: Features go in, the label comes out, the identifier stays out
slides.text: Three kinds of column Features go in, the label comes out, the identifier stays out Features What is known when the prediction is made: wound area, layers, diabetic. Written X. Label What you want to predict, known for past rows only: ran over 40 minutes. Written y. Identifier Which visit or client a row is about. Needed to join and audit, useless as a predictor. Ask of every column. Is it known at the moment the prediction is made? If not, it is not a feature, however well it predicts.

slides.title: A rule is a function from features to a prediction
slides.text: A prediction rule A rule is a function from features to a prediction def rule(visit) -> bool: return visit["area_cm2"] >= 15 On the six visits it flags 4 and catches all 3 that ran over One flag was needless: the 28.5 cm² wound with one layer A model is the same thing, written by a fitting procedure from many rows instead of by you from six

slides.title: A screen makes two different mistakes
slides.text: Scoring a rule A screen makes two different mistakes A miss The visit ran over and the rule did not flag it. For a fall screen: a client who falls and got no programme. A needless flag The rule flagged a visit that was fine. For a fall screen: a programme for a client who would not have fallen. What goes wrong. Counting only "right answers" mixes the two, and a rule that flags nobody can look excellent when the outcome is rare.

slides.title: Score a rule on rows you did not write it from
slides.text: Where to score Score a rule on rows you did not write it from 1 · Look at a few rows and write a rule → 2 · Apply it to many rows you never looked at → 3 · Count misses and needless flags there Takeaway. A rule always looks best on the rows that inspired it.

slides.title: A dataframe holds the table; a library holds the models
slides.text: The tools A dataframe holds the table; a library holds the models import pandas as pd visits = pd.read_csv("visits.csv") X = visits[["area_cm2", "layers"]] y = visits["over_40"] visits.apply(rule, axis=1) # one answer per row A dataframe library (pandas, Polars) reads and slices tables A machine learning library (scikit-learn, tidymodels in R) fits and applies models The labs give you helpers for loading; you write the parts that matter

slides.title: Which column belongs in the fall-risk rule?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which column belongs in the fall-risk rule? An analyst at a home-care company lists four columns for a rule that runs at the end of the nurse's assessment visit. Which one may the rule use? The client's code Seconds the client took to walk four metres in the visit Whether the client called for help in the following month Whether the client fell in the following six months

slides.title: A screening rule by hand
slides.text: Lab 1.1 · 35 min A screening rule by hand Write a fall-risk rule on paper for ten clients, turn it into a function and count its misses and needless flags on 1,000 assessments D1_1_hand_rule.ipynb Read the ten rows: name the identifier, the features and the label 5 min Write a rule on paper that flags a client and apply it to the ten rows 8 min Turn the rule into a Python function 7 min Count its errors on 1,000 training assessments: missed fallers and needless flags 10 min Compare with a colleague's rule and with flagging nobody 5 min ✱ Stretch: Give your rule one number you can tune and find its best value on the training rows

slides.title: Loss and gradient descent
slides.text: Session 2 Loss and gradient descent Compute a mean squared error by hand for a candidate line Take a gradient step by hand and say why the loss falls Run gradient descent in code and read its loss curve 02

slides.title: Flagging nobody was right most often and found no faller
slides.text: Lab 1.1 debrief Flagging nobody was right most often and found no faller Rule, on 1,000 training assessments Caught Missed Needless Right A fall in the past year, or a walk of 8 s or more 73 77 153 770 A walk of 7 s or more 62 88 188 724 Flag nobody 0 150 0 850 Lab 1.1 reference run: 150 of the 1,000 clients fell within six months.

slides.title: A loss turns "how wrong is this rule" into one number
slides.text: From writing rules to fitting them A loss turns "how wrong is this rule" into one number Pick a family of rules with a few numbers in it: a line minutes = w × area + b For one setting of w and b, compute the error on every example Average the squared errors: the mean squared error Fitting means finding the numbers with the lowest loss Same idea, every model. A line, a logistic regression, a neural network and a language model are all fitted by making a loss small.

slides.title: Five wound-care visits, two candidate lines
slides.text: A worked loss Five wound-care visits, two candidate lines Area (cm²) Minutes Error of w 1.0, b 15 Error of w 1.2, b 15 4 20 -1.0 -0.2 8 26 -3.0 -1.4 12 27 0.0 2.4 16 33 -2.0 1.2 20 39 -4.0 0.0 Mean squared error 6.00 1.84 Error is prediction minus actual. Synthetic visits (teaching_examples.py, D1 S2).

slides.title: For a line, the loss is a bowl over w and b
slides.text: The shape of the loss For a line, the loss is a bowl over w and b Loss against the slope: a bowl with one bottom slope w loss lowest loss The tangent at the red point slopes down to the right, so the step goes right.

slides.title: Step against the slope, by a small rate
slides.text: Gradient descent Step against the slope, by a small rate e = w * x + b - y # errors slope_w = 2 * mean(e * x) slope_b = 2 * mean(e) w = w - rate * slope_w b = b - rate * slope_b From w 1.0, b 15 on the five visits slope_w = -56.0, slope_b = -4.0. With rate 0.002 the step gives w 1.112, b 15.008 and a loss of 1.93, down from 6.00. The exact bottom Least squares gives w 1.125, b 15.5 and a loss of 1.50. More steps keep closing the gap.

slides.title: The learning rate decides whether the steps arrive
slides.text: The one setting The learning rate decides whether the steps arrive Too small Every step is safe and the walk takes forever. About right The loss falls fast, then flattens as the slopes flatten near the bottom. Too large Each step jumps over the bottom to a higher wall; the loss grows without end. What goes wrong. A loss curve that rises or turns into "nan" almost always means the rate is too large or a feature has huge values.

slides.title: Plot the loss after every step and read three things
slides.text: Reading a loss curve Plot the loss after every step and read three things Falling : the steps are working Flat : you are near the bottom, or the rate is far too small Rising or jagged : the rate is too large Use a log scale on the loss axis: the early drop is huge, the late gains small

slides.title: Which way does the step move the slope?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which way does the step move the slope? A line predicts dressing minutes from wound area. At the current line the slope of the loss in w is -40 and the rate is 0.01. What does one gradient step do to w? It lowers w by 0.4 It raises w by 40 It raises w by 0.4 It leaves w where it is

slides.title: Two gradient steps on ten rows
slides.text: Lab 1.2 · 35 min Two gradient steps on ten rows Fit a line for visit minutes from the number of medicines: a loss by hand, two gradient steps by hand, then a few thousand in code D1_2_gradient_steps.ipynb Guess a line for visit minutes and compute its mean squared error by hand 8 min Write mse(w, b) and check your hand number 5 min Take two gradient steps by hand from w = 0 and b = 0 10 min Run 2,000 steps in code and plot the loss 7 min Compare with the exact least-squares line 5 min ✱ Stretch: Raise the learning rate until the loss explodes, and explain why

slides.title: Nearest neighbours and linear models by hand
slides.text: Session 3 Nearest neighbours and linear models by hand Classify a new client by a vote of its nearest neighbours, by hand Explain why the scale of a feature changes the neighbours Fit a least-squares line from means by hand and reproduce it in code 03

slides.title: Two steps took the loss from 1,757 to 123; two thousand reached 49
slides.text: Lab 1.2 debrief Two steps took the loss from 1,757 to 123; two thousand reached 49 Line for visit minutes w (min per medicine) b (min) Loss Start 0 0 1,757.1 After step 1 5.008 0.798 195.6 After step 2 6.072 1.029 123.4 After 2,000 steps 3.752 19.263 48.98 Exact least squares 3.752 19.267 48.98 Lab 1.2 reference run on the ten rows, rate 0.01. Slopes at the start: -500.8 and -79.8.

slides.title: Keep the examples, or keep a summary of them
slides.text: Two ways to use examples Keep the examples, or keep a summary of them Nearest neighbours Keep every row. For a new case, find the most similar rows and let them vote. No fitting; all the work happens when you predict. A linear model Fit a few numbers once, then throw the rows away. Prediction is a sum of features times weights.

slides.title: Similar means close: a distance over the features
slides.text: Nearest neighbours Similar means close: a distance over the features Area (cm²) Layers Over 40 Distance to (10, 1) 5 1 0 5.00 6 3 0 4.47 18 2 1 8.06 20 4 1 10.44 9 4 1 3.16 22 1 0 12.00 Distance = √(area difference² + layers difference²) The three nearest (highlighted) vote 0, 0, 1 Prediction for a 10 cm² wound with one layer: will not run over Six synthetic visits (teaching_examples.py, D1 S3).

slides.title: Change a unit and the neighbours change
slides.text: The trap in distances Change a unit and the neighbours change Record the same wounds in square metres: 10 cm² becomes 0.001 m² Area differences shrink to almost nothing; layers decide every distance The three nearest become the rows with one or two layers: rows 1, 6 and 3 in place of 5, 2 and 1 Nothing about the wounds changed, only a unit What goes wrong. A distance adds raw differences, so the column with the biggest numbers wins. Scale the columns first (Day 3).

slides.title: For one feature, the best line comes from means
slides.text: A line by hand For one feature, the best line comes from means w = Σ (x − mean x)(y − mean y) ÷ Σ (x − mean x)² b = mean y − w × mean x The bottom of the bowl, found in one move instead of many steps. The five wound visits mean area 12, mean minutes 29. The formula gives w 1.125 and b 15.5: the same line gradient descent was walking towards.

slides.title: Every scikit-learn model has the same two moves
slides.text: The same two models in code Every scikit-learn model has the same two moves from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression knn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=3).fit(X, y) # stores the rows knn.predict(new_rows) # votes line = LinearRegression().fit(X[["area_cm2"]], minutes) line.coef_, line.intercept_ # w and b

slides.title: Why did the neighbours change?
slides.text: Checkpoint Why did the neighbours change? A colleague switched the "walk" column of a neighbour model from seconds to milliseconds, and the three nearest clients of a new client changed. What happened? The walk now has far larger numbers, so it dominates every distance The clients' walks were measured again The model's weights were refitted The colleague changed k

slides.title: Two models by hand, then in code
slides.text: Lab 1.3 · 40 min Two models by hand, then in code Fit two models by hand, then reproduce them in code: a three-nearest-neighbour vote and a least-squares line on the ten-row table D1_3_two_models_by_hand.ipynb By hand: distances from two new clients to the ten rows and a three-neighbour vote 10 min Rescale walk seconds and see whether the vote changes 6 min By hand: the least-squares line for visit minutes from medicines, from means 10 min Reproduce both models with scikit-learn and compare with your paper 8 min Write three sentences on how each model turned examples into a rule 6 min ✱ Stretch: Repeat the vote with k = 1 and k = 5 and say which you trust

slides.title: Tenths of a second flipped both votes; the line matched to the last digit
slides.text: Lab 1.3 debrief Tenths of a second flipped both votes; the line matched to the last digit Three-neighbour vote Client P Client Q Walk in seconds fall no fall Walk in tenths no fall fall Visit minutes from medicines By hand and by LinearRegression: w 3.752, b 19.267. The same line Lab 1.2 reached by steps. Lab 1.3 reference run. P: one recorded fall, 6.8 s; Q: none, 6.0 s.

slides.title: What matters is the score on clients the model has not seen
slides.text: Generalisation What matters is the score on clients the model has not seen A model is built from past rows and used on future clients Its score on its own training rows is always flattering Hold some rows back, never fit on them, and score there The gap between the two scores is the first thing to look at (Day 2)

slides.title: Train on one, choose on another, report on a third
slides.text: Three sets, three jobs Train on one, choose on another, report on a third Training Every model is fitted here. Seen as often as you like. Validation Compare models and settings here. Each choice makes its score a little flattering. Test Opened once, after every choice. Its score is the one you report. What goes wrong. Look at the test score, change something, look again: the test set has become a second validation set.

slides.title: Split by date when the model will meet the future
slides.text: How to split Split by date when the model will meet the future Training the oldest months → Validation the next months → Test the most recent months The wound-care visits: 24 months, split at month 14 and month 19 into 1,390, 535 and 475 visits.

slides.title: Always score the model that does nothing
slides.text: The first comparison Always score the model that does nothing 0.914 validation accuracy of "no visit runs over 50 minutes" 0.940 validation accuracy of a logistic regression Wound-care visits, label "over 50 minutes" (8% of visits); teaching_examples.py, D1 S4.

slides.title: AUC: how often a positive case outscores a negative one
slides.text: A score for ranking AUC: how often a positive case outscores a negative one A model gives each row a score between 0 and 1 Pick one visit that ran over and one that did not, at random AUC is the chance the first gets the higher score 0.5 is a coin; the do-nothing baseline scores exactly 0.5 The wound-care logistic regression: 0.968

slides.title: A baseline, a line and a tree, on the same split
slides.text: The lab's comparison A baseline, a line and a tree, on the same split models = { "baseline": DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent"), "logistic regression": make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression()), "decision tree": DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=4, random_state=SEED), } # fit each on training rows, score each on validation, choose, then test once

slides.title: Which score goes in the report?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which score goes in the report? An analyst trains five models for a wound-care screen, keeps the one with the best validation AUC (0.91), then scores the test set once (0.88). Which number describes how the screen will do next year? 0.91, the validation AUC The mean of the two, about 0.90 The training AUC, which is higher still 0.88, the test AUC

slides.title: Baseline, line and tree on a fixed split
slides.text: Lab 1.4 · 40 min Baseline, line and tree on a fixed split Compare a baseline, a logistic regression and a tree on the fixed split by date, then score the test set once D1_4_three_way_split.ipynb Load the split and check sizes and base rates 5 min Score a baseline that predicts no fall 5 min Fit a logistic regression and a tree 8 min Compare on validation: accuracy and ranking 10 min Choose on validation, score test once 7 min Write the results table 5 min ✱ Stretch: Split at random instead of by date and compare

slides.title: Three things to keep
slides.text: Day 1 · wrap-up Three things to keep A model is a rule Features in, a prediction out. Fitting picks the rule's numbers by making a loss small. Two kinds of error A miss and a needless flag cost different things; counting right answers hides both. Held out, once Train, choose on validation, report the test score you opened once, against a baseline.

slides.title: Generalisation and measuring
slides.text: Today Generalisation and measuring Session 1 · Model complexity, overfitting and regularisation More capacity fits the training rows better and new rows worse past a point; regularisation pulls it back Session 2 · Cross-validation and learning curves Several folds show how much a score moves; a learning curve shows whether more data would help Session 3 · Confusion matrix, precision and recall Four counts behind every classification score, and why accuracy hides a lazy model Session 4 · Thresholds, error costs and base rates The threshold is a decision: it follows from what each error costs and how common the outcome is

slides.title: What did fitting do yesterday?
slides.text: Day 1 review What did fitting do yesterday? A colleague says: "Fitting the wound-care line means the computer searched for the line that passes through the most points." What is the accurate version? It finds the line that passes through every point It uses the rule the nurse wrote down It finds the numbers with the lowest mean squared error It picks the line with the best test score

slides.title: Model complexity, overfitting and regularisation
slides.text: Session 1 Model complexity, overfitting and regularisation Produce training and validation curves over model complexity Tell underfitting from overfitting on a plotted curve Use a regularisation setting to reduce overfitting 01

slides.title: Accuracy barely moved; the ranking score did
slides.text: Lab 1.4 debrief Accuracy barely moved; the ranking score did On validation (1,263 assessments) Accuracy AUC Baseline: nobody falls 0.838 0.500 Logistic regression 0.842 0.739 Decision tree, depth 4 0.834 0.682 Lab 1.4 reference run. Chosen on validation: the logistic regression; test, opened once: accuracy 0.841, AUC 0.732.

slides.title: A flexible model can learn the noise as well as the pattern
slides.text: Model complexity A flexible model can learn the noise as well as the pattern A tree's depth is how many questions it may ask; each extra level doubles the possible groups With enough depth, every training row gets its own leaf: training error reaches zero Overfitting: training score keeps rising while the validation score falls Underfitting: both scores are low; the model is too simple to show the pattern In the case Two clients with the same walk time and the same falls can have different outcomes. A tree that separates them is memorising chance.

slides.title: Wound care: deeper trees, then a falling validation score
slides.text: A parallel example Wound care: deeper trees, then a falling validation score Tree depth Training Validation 1 .941 .927 2 .949 .935 4 .958 .935 8 .983 .923 12 .999 .923 no limit 1.000 .916 Read the gap. The gap between the columns grows with depth; choose the depth where validation peaks, not training. Accuracy on synthetic wound-care visits (predict a visit over 50 minutes), seed 7, from labs/_tools/teaching_examples.py. Depth 3 gives .953 and .935; depth 6 gives .969 and .929.

slides.title: A penalty on large weights keeps a model simpler
slides.text: Regularisation A penalty on large weights keeps a model simpler Add to the loss a cost for large weights: the model trades fit for simplicity In scikit-learn's logistic regression, C is the inverse: small C, strong penalty For trees, the penalty is a limit: max_depth, min_samples_leaf The strength is chosen on validation, like depth Same picture, other dial Strong penalty: underfit. No penalty with many features: overfit. The best setting sits between.

slides.title: Which depth do you report?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which depth do you report? For a wound-care screen, a tree of depth 12 has training accuracy 0.999 and validation 0.923; a tree of depth 3 has 0.953 and 0.935. Which do you choose, and why? Depth 12, because its training score is higher Depth 3, because its validation score is higher Whichever does better on the test set Depth 12, because its average of the two is higher

slides.title: Several folds show how much a score moves by chance
slides.text: Cross-validation Several folds show how much a score moves by chance 1 · Cut the training rows into five folds → 2 · Rotate fit on four, score the fifth, five times → 3 · Report the mean and the spread of five scores Repeat clients. If one client's visits sit in two folds, the model is scored on someone it has seen. Group the folds by client.

slides.title: Wound care: five grouped folds, one spread
slides.text: A parallel example Wound care: five grouped folds, one spread Fold AUC 1 0.903 2 0.932 3 0.920 4 0.960 5 0.917 0.927 ± 0.019 mean and standard deviation of the five folds Logistic regression on the synthetic wound-care visits, folds grouped by client.

slides.title: Training and validation scores as the rows grow
slides.text: Learning curves Training and validation scores as the rows grow Good fit The two curves meet at a useful score. More rows help a little. Overfit Training stays near perfect, validation well below. More rows or a simpler model help. Underfit Both curves meet low. More rows do not help; better features or a richer model do. A question to ask. Will collecting more assessments help? The curve answers before anyone collects them.

slides.title: Is the new model better?
slides.text: Checkpoint Is the new model better? On the wound-care screen, five grouped folds give a mean AUC of 0.927 with a spread of 0.019. A new model scores 0.931 on the same folds. What do you conclude? The new model is better and should replace the old one The new model is worse, because it is more complex Regroup the folds by sector and score again They are tied; prefer the simpler one

slides.title: Confusion matrix, precision and recall
slides.text: Session 3 Confusion matrix, precision and recall Fill the four cells of a confusion matrix by hand Compute precision, recall and specificity from the cells Explain why accuracy misleads at a low base rate 03

slides.title: Five folds spread from 0.568 to 0.704
slides.text: Lab 2.2 debrief Five folds spread from 0.568 to 0.704 Grouped folds on 1,486 training clients (585 with repeat visits): mean AUC 0.657, spread 0.047 The single validation score was 0.682: one draw from a wide range The logistic regression's learning curve met near 0.73 to 0.74: a good fit; more rows add little Curve Label A, B overfit, underfit C, D good fit, underfit E, F overfit, overfit

slides.title: Four cells: caught, needless, missed and correctly passed
slides.text: The confusion matrix Four cells: caught, needless, missed and correctly passed Flagged Not flagged Fell caught (true positive, TP) missed (false negative, FN) Did not fall needless (false positive, FP) correct pass (true negative, TN) A threshold makes the flag. A model gives a score from 0 to 1; flag when the score is at or above the threshold. Change it and the four cells change.

slides.title: Precision and recall answer two different questions
slides.text: Rates from the cells Precision and recall answer two different questions Recall = TP / (TP + FN) Of those who fell, the share we flagged. Low recall: fallers missed. Precision = TP / (TP + FP) Of those we flagged, the share who fell. Low precision: programmes wasted. Specificity = TN / (TN + FP): of those who did not fall, the share left alone Accuracy = (TP + TN) / all: dominated by the larger group when one outcome is rare

slides.title: Wound care at 0.5: accuracy 0.940, recall 0.435
slides.text: A parallel example Wound care at 0.5: accuracy 0.940, recall 0.435 535 visits Flagged Not flagged Over 50 min 20 26 Not over 6 483 Precision 20 / 26 = 0.769 Recall 20 / 46 = 0.435 Specificity 483 / 489 = 0.988 At threshold 0.2: recall 0.783, precision 0.600, accuracy 0.936

slides.title: What does this screen miss?
slides.text: Checkpoint What does this screen miss? A wound-care screen flags 30 of 500 visits; 24 of the 30 ran long, and 60 visits ran long in all. What is its recall? 0.40: it caught 24 of the 60 long visits 0.80: 24 of the 30 flagged visits ran long 0.06: it flagged 30 of the 500 visits 0.92: it was right on 458 of the 500 visits

slides.title: Thresholds, error costs and base rates
slides.text: Session 4 Thresholds, error costs and base rates Compute the expected cost of a threshold from the confusion matrix and two costs Choose a threshold on validation scores and report it on test scores Explain how a change in the base rate moves the cost of a threshold 04

slides.title: At 0.5, the fall screen was 84% accurate and missed 188 of 205 fallers
slides.text: Lab 2.3 debrief At 0.5, the fall screen was 84% accurate and missed 188 of 205 fallers Validation at 0.5 Flagged Not Fell 17 188 Did not fall 12 1,046 Recall 0.083, precision 0.586 Accuracy 0.842, against 0.838 for flagging nobody Twenty rows at 0.2: 2 caught, 3 needless, 1 missed, 14 right

slides.title: Choose the threshold with the lowest expected cost
slides.text: Error costs Choose the threshold with the lowest expected cost Give each error a cost in the same units: a missed outcome C_FN, a needless flag C_FP Expected cost = C_FN × FN + C_FP × FP, per 1,000 clients Try thresholds on validation; keep the cheapest; report it once on test The owner of the decision sets the costs; the analyst shows the trade-off A rule of thumb. If scores are well calibrated, flag when the score exceeds C_FP / (C_FP + C_FN).

slides.title: Wound care: a missed long visit costs four short ones
slides.text: A parallel example Wound care: a missed long visit costs four short ones Threshold Cost per 1,000 Flagged 0.1 112 0.161 0.2 120 0.112 0.3 159 0.077 0.5 206 0.049 Rule and search can differ. The search on validation found 0.1; the rule of thumb, 1 / (1 + 4), says 0.2. The rule assumes calibrated scores. Costs 4 for a missed long visit and 1 for a needless slot.

slides.title: The same screen gives a different precision where the outcome is more common
slides.text: Base rates The same screen gives a different precision where the outcome is more common The base rate is the share with the outcome, before any model Same scores, more fallers: more of the flagged are fallers, so precision rises The cheapest threshold moves too, because misses happen more often What goes wrong A precision measured in one sector is quoted for another with twice the base rate. Report the base rate with every precision.

slides.title: What does the rule of thumb give?
slides.text: Checkpoint What does the rule of thumb give? For a wound-care screen, a missed long visit costs 9 units and a needless extra slot costs 1. With calibrated scores, above which score should a visit be flagged? 0.5 9 0.1 0.9

slides.text: Day 2 · wrap-up Three things to keep Choose on validation Training scores always favour flexibility. The validation peak is the choice. Scores have a spread Grouped folds show how much a score moves; smaller differences are ties. Costs set the threshold Four cells, two costs and the base rate decide what to flag; 0.5 is a default, not a decision.

slides.title: The cheapest threshold was 0.17, far from 0.5
slides.text: Lab 2.4 debrief The cheapest threshold was 0.17, far from 0.5 Per 1,000 validation clients, costs 6 and 1 Cost Flag nobody 974 Threshold 0.5 903 Flag everyone 838 The rule of thumb, 1/7 = 0.143 571 Cheapest on validation, 0.17 544 On test at 0.17: 32% flagged, recall 0.608, precision 0.322. With the base rate raised to 0.291, the cheapest threshold fell to 0.07.

slides.title: For a number, measure how far off, on average
slides.text: Regression For a number, measure how far off, on average MAE , mean absolute error: the typical miss, in the target's units RMSE , root mean squared error: like MAE, but large misses weigh more RMSE is never below MAE; a big gap means a few large misses Always compare with a naive baseline: predict the training mean, or the median Five errors, by hand Errors 3, −2, 10, −1, 0 minutes. MAE = 16 / 5 = 3.20. RMSE = √(114 / 5) = 4.77. The 10 pulls RMSE up.

slides.text: Lab 3.2 debrief Scaling helped the neighbour model; the full pipeline scored 0.744 BMI was blank in 6.1% of training rows; 83 validation rows were filled with the training median, 27.7 Fifty nearest neighbours: AUC 0.647 unscaled, 0.683 scaled The column transformer and a logistic regression: 15 inputs, validation AUC 0.744

slides.title: Fit every step on training rows, inside the pipeline
slides.text: The rule Fit every step on training rows, inside the pipeline 1 · Split first before any step learns anything → 2 · Fit the pipeline scaling, filling, selection, model: on training rows → 3 · Apply the fitted pipeline to validation and test In cross-validation too. The whole pipeline goes inside the folds, so each fold prepares from its own training part.

slides.title: Noise columns, selected on all rows, looked useful
slides.text: A parallel example Noise columns, selected on all rows, looked useful 150 wound-care visits, 600 columns of pure noise, keep the 10 best Selection on all rows, then cross-validation: AUC 0.783 Selection inside the pipeline: AUC 0.439, no better than chance Why it happens With 600 columns, some match the labels by luck. Choosing them with every label in view, then scoring on the same labels, rewards the luck.

slides.title: Which number is honest?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which number is honest? A wound-care analyst keeps the 20 best of 900 sensor columns, chosen on all 200 visits, then reports a cross-validated AUC of 0.81. What should a reviewer ask for? The same procedure with ten folds in place of five A random forest in place of the logistic regression The selection inside the pipeline, refitted in every fold The 5 best columns in place of the 20 best

slides.title: Selection before the split turned noise into an AUC of 0.838
slides.text: Lab 3.3 debrief Selection before the split turned noise into an AUC of 0.838 Sensor pilot, 240 clients, 400 noise columns Before the split In the pipeline Real labels 0.838 0.457 Shuffled labels 0.904 0.533 Scaling fitted on all rows against training rows: 0.7403 and 0.7403. Scaling leaked nothing measurable here; selection leaked a great deal.

slides.title: Three leaks a pipeline does not catch
slides.text: Leakage Three leaks a pipeline does not catch Target leak A column recorded after the outcome, often because of it: a treatment started because the event happened. Duplicate leak The same row on both sides of the split; the model is scored on rows it has seen. Temporal leak A column, or the split, that uses what happened after the prediction date. Not rare. Kapoor and Narayanan found leakage in 329 published papers across 17 fields.

slides.title: Four questions before trusting a score
slides.text: A checklist Four questions before trusting a score When is each column recorded? Read the data dictionary; anything after the prediction date goes Does one column alone rank almost perfectly? Score each alone; a very good one deserves the first question Are there copies? Count repeated identifiers, and test rows with a twin in training Does the split match use? The screen predicts next year, so train on the past and test on the latest period

slides.title: Which column is the leak?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which column is the leak? A screen predicts whether a wound will be infected within 30 days of a visit. Alone, one column ranks infected wounds with an AUC of 0.93. Which column is most likely a leak? Wound area, measured at the visit An antibiotic prescription, updated over the 30 days The client's diabetes status, at registration The number of past wounds, counted at the visit

slides.text: Day 3 review Which split matches use? A wound-care screen will score next year's visits. The analyst has three years of dated visits, many clients with several. Which split gives an honest test score? Train on the first two years, test on the third A random 70/30 split of all visits Train on the last two years, test on the first A random split of clients, all years mixed

slides.title: The analyst's 0.936 became an honest 0.732
slides.text: Lab 3.4 debrief The analyst's 0.936 became an honest 0.732 Leak Evidence in the reference run Target: physio_referral AUC alone 0.880; updated during the six months after the visit Duplicate: the random split 573 repeated rows; 236 of 1,605 test rows also in training Temporal: client_falls_total, the split 10.7% of rows count later visits; 30.2% of training rows from 2025 Lab 3.4 reference run. The best clinical feature alone, walk_seconds, scored 0.687.

slides.title: Each family draws the boundary between flag and pass differently
slides.text: Three families Each family draws the boundary between flag and pass differently Linear model A weighted sum of the inputs; the boundary is a straight line, or a flat plane. Each weight can be read. Decision tree Yes-or-no questions on one input at a time; the boundary is a staircase of boxes. Small neural network Several weighted sums, each bent, then summed again; the boundary can curve. All fitted the same way. The line and the network by gradient steps on a loss, as on Day 1; the tree by choosing one split at a time.

slides.title: A fixed seed makes a run repeatable, not certain
slides.text: Reproducibility A fixed seed makes a run repeatable, not certain A network starts from random weights; a tree breaks ties at random: the seed fixes those draws Same seed, same data, same library versions: the same numbers, every time Another seed gives a slightly different model: that change is part of the result's uncertainty Two models closer than the seed-to-seed change are tied What goes wrong. A notebook that only works when its cells are run in one hidden order. Restart and run all before reporting.

slides.title: What do you report?
slides.text: Checkpoint What do you report? On a wound-care screen, a small network scores a validation AUC of 0.873 with seed 1 and 0.866 with seed 2; a logistic regression scores 0.869. Which choice is best supported? The network, quoting its seed 1 score of 0.873 The network, because its mean is 0.0005 higher The logistic regression, because they are tied Whichever scores higher on the test set

slides.text: Session 2 Distribution shift Compare a later batch with the training rows feature by feature Measure a screen's flag rate and recall by sector on a later batch Name a shift and the check that would have caught it 02

slides.title: The network tied with the logistic regression
slides.text: Lab 4.1 debrief The network tied with the logistic regression Validation AUC, seed 101 AUC Baseline 0.500 Logistic regression 0.744 Decision tree, depth 4 0.685 Small neural network, 16 units 0.743 Seed 7 gave the network 0.743 again. Chosen: the logistic regression; test AUC, opened once: 0.731.

slides.title: A model meets rows unlike its training rows
slides.text: Distribution shift A model meets rows unlike its training rows New people A new sector, older clients, a new referral route: the inputs' mix changes. A changed measurement A new device, unit or protocol: the same client gets a different number. A changed outcome rate More or fewer events than in training: precision and the cheapest threshold move. The model cannot tell you. It scores whatever it is given. The checks must be built around it.

slides.title: Cheap checks catch shifts in the first week
slides.text: Monitoring Cheap checks catch shifts in the first week Share flagged , by sector and by month, against the training period The mean of each input , by sector and by month, against the training period Recall and precision once the outcomes arrive, months later An owner for each alert, and a person who decides on a pause A parallel example. A new wound clinic records area in cm², not mm²: every area is 100 times smaller. Its mean area, and its flag rate, would show it on the first day.

slides.title: Which check comes first?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which check comes first? A wound-care screen goes live in a new clinic on Sunday. Outcomes take 30 days to arrive. Which check can warn of a problem in the first week? The clinic's recall at the threshold The clinic's AUC on its first week of visits Retraining the model on the clinic's visits The clinic's share flagged and input means

slides.title: One threshold can give different recall to different groups

slides.title: Leaving an attribute out does not remove it
slides.text: Proxies Leaving an attribute out does not remove it A proxy is an input that carries a sensitive attribute: a first name, a home address, a job title Test it: predict the attribute from the input; compare with guessing the larger group An input can also be recorded differently for one group, so the model is weaker for that group even with no proxy What goes wrong. "The model does not use sex, so it cannot treat men and women differently." Measure, then say.

slides.title: The SDAIA AI Ethics Principles: fairness through the model's life
slides.text: National reference The SDAIA AI Ethics Principles: fairness through the model's life Preparing input data: sensitive attributes are not model inputs unless there is a justification Building and validating: the chosen model's fairness metrics fall within a defined threshold Deploying and monitoring: the predefined fairness metrics are monitored in production Course rule. Also test for proxies of a sensitive attribute. The English edition names this step and the Arabic edition does not, so the course states it as its own rule.

slides.title: One page that says what the model is for, and for whom it is weak
slides.text: The model card One page that says what the model is for, and for whom it is weak Intended use and out of scope Data, split and metrics, against a baseline Metrics by group, with counts Known limits and who should not rely on it Monitoring: what, how often, by whom Prepared, reviewed, accepted The analyst prepares it; a different person reviews it; the owner of the decision accepts the model for use.

slides.title: Two parts of 60 minutes, on paper, without devices
